title: Meditations
author: Marcus Aurelius
openingText: From my grandfather Verus I learned good character and control of my temper. From my father's reputation and my memory of him: modesty and a manly character. From my mother: reverence for the gods and generosity; holding back not only from doing wrong, but even from thinking of it; and also a simple way of living, far removed from the habits of the rich. From my great-grandfather: not to have been sent to the public schools open to everyone, but to have had good teachers at home, and to know that on an education like this one should spend generously.
about:
Marcus Aurelius, Roman emperor from 161 to 180 CE, wrote these reflections in Greek for himself. At least part of the work comes from his years on military campaigns. Its twelve books move between gratitude, anger, duty, death and the place of a human life in the universe.

This is a working notebook rather than a systematic introduction to Stoicism. Marcus returns to the same problems because knowing a principle and living by it are different things. He tells himself to question his first impressions, act justly toward others and accept what he cannot determine. His repeated reminders also make demanding claims: that moral character matters more than pleasure or pain, and that each person belongs to a larger community.

Read a few entries at a time, but keep their context in view. The striking sentences are parts of arguments, exercises and ancient beliefs about nature. Marcus's ideas can be useful to think with without becoming rules you must accept. Notice especially how often the call for self-command leads back to patience, cooperation and care for other people.

angleCards.title: A ruler examining himself
angleCards.text: Marcus reminds himself to resist flattery, anger and the habits of imperial power. Read his advice alongside the authority he possessed.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how Marcus's position as emperor shapes his demands on himself.

angleCards.title: Stoicism in daily practice
angleCards.text: Follow the movement from an irritating event to a judgment about it, and from that judgment to a possible response.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to understand how Marcus turns Stoic ideas into exercises in attention and action.

angleCards.title: Living with a limited time
angleCards.text: Death, forgotten reputations and the passing of generations recur throughout the book. Ask what each reminder is meant to change in the present.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to trace how awareness of death shapes Marcus's ideas about time, ambition and duty.

angleCards.title: The individual and the whole
angleCards.text: Hands, branches, bees and citizens illustrate our dependence on one another. Consider where those images clarify his ethics and where they invite questions.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to explore Marcus's argument that caring for others belongs to human nature.

cast.name: Marcus Aurelius
cast.description: Roman emperor and the voice addressing itself throughout the book. His reminders concern his own judgments and conduct, including the temptations attached to power.

cast.name: Antoninus Pius
cast.description: Marcus's predecessor as emperor. Book 1 praises his steadiness, careful decisions and restraint; Book 6 returns to him as a practical example.

cast.name: Epictetus
cast.description: A Stoic teacher whose writings Marcus encountered through Rusticus. Marcus quotes him repeatedly, especially toward the end of Book 11.

cast.name: Junius Rusticus
cast.description: Marcus credits him with encouraging careful reading, plain speech and attention to character, and with sharing Epictetus's writings.

cast.name: Diognetus
cast.description: In Book 1 Marcus thanks him for encouraging an interest in philosophy and resistance to superstition and empty distractions.

cast.name: Logos
cast.description: A philosophical idea rather than a character. Marcus links human reason with the rational order of the whole and asks how individual conduct can agree with it.

whyItMatters.title: An account of moral practice
whyItMatters.body: The repeated return to familiar questions lets us watch someone trying to make a philosophy habitual. A reminder about anger can become an argument about how other people think; a thought about death can become a reason to do today's work well. The movement between principle and particular situation is central to the book.

whyItMatters.title: Power and responsibility
whyItMatters.body: A ruler's private instruction to himself is not proof that his public conduct always matched his ideals. The gap is worth examining. Marcus asks for restraint, truthfulness and cooperation while writing from a position that gave him unusual power over other lives.

whyItMatters.title: A demanding idea of community
whyItMatters.body: The book repeatedly asks us to see others as relatives and fellow citizens of a larger world. Its concern with inner freedom does not end in withdrawal: Marcus also insists on useful action, justice and kindness. That tension gives readers something more substantial to consider than isolated motivational sayings.
